metadata.title: Case Study: Post-Operative Pulmonary Embolism (Critical Care Level 5).

quickStart.summary: Management of a 68-year-old female developing acute pulmonary embolism on POD 3 after total hip arthroplasty.

content.chiefComplaint: Sudden onset of 'sharp' chest pain and severe shortness of breath.

nursesNotes.note: Client suddenly reported 'stabbing' chest pain. Appears extremely anxious (impending doom). Diaphoretic and tachypneic. O2 sat dropped to 86%. Lung sounds clear bilaterally. Rapid Response Team (RRT) called.

clinicalData.historyPhysical: 68yo female POD 3 status-post right total hip arthroplasty. Surgery was uncomplicated. Client has been slow to ambulate due to pain. Suddenly developed acute distress at 11:20 while sitting in chair. No prior history of VTE. Leg assessment reveals slight swelling of the right calf compared to left.

history.note: Client suddenly reported 'stabbing' chest pain. Appears extremely anxious (impending doom). Diaphoretic and tachypneic. O2 sat dropped to 86%. Lung sounds clear bilaterally. Rapid Response Team (RRT) called.

rationale.coreConcept: Acute Pulmonary Embolism (PE) is a life-threatening complication of immobility following major orthopedic surgery.
rationale.caseSummary: Evelyn Graves demonstrates the classic triad of sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, and hypoxemia. Her elevated D-Dimer and troponin, combined with respiratory alkalosis (compensatory hyperventilation), strongly indicate PE with potential right heart strain.
rationale.answerAnalysis: See option review for detailed analysis.
rationale.trap: Failure to recognize that 'clear lung sounds' in the presence of severe hypoxia is often a hallmark of PE (it is a ventilation/perfusion mismatch, not an airway obstruction).
rationale.goldenRule: Always assume Pulmonary Embolism in any post-operative patient with sudden-onset respiratory distress and sharp chest pain until proven otherwise.

difficulty.label: Evaluation.
difficulty.clinicalStrategy: Prioritize rapid assessment of perfusion vs ventilation markers.

mnemonic.title: STOP-VTE
mnemonic.content: S: Sudden Onset; T: Tachycardia; O: Oxygen Drop; P: Pleuritic Pain; V: Venous Stasis.
mnemonic.explanation: These are the five hallmarks of a post-operative embolic event.

cheatSheet.title: PE Management Protocol.
points: Stabilize: High-flow oxygen (NRB) is the first action.
Anticoagulate: Heparin drip initiated immediately once confirmed.
Surveillance: Monitor for RV strain (JVD, Hypotension, Troponin).
Confirmation: CT Pulmonary Angiography (CTPA) is the gold standard.

referenceInfo.anatomy: The pulmonary artery system and right ventricle interaction.
referenceInfo.physiology: V/Q Mismatch: Perfusion is blocked while ventilation continues, leading to dead-space ventilation.
referenceInfo.pharm: Unfractionated Heparin (prevents clot propagation) vs. Thrombolytics (dissolves clot).

rationale.clinicalStrategy: Prioritize rapid assessment of perfusion vs ventilation markers.

screens.prompt: Highlight the clinical findings that most strongly suggest an embolic event.
screens.text: The client reports stabbing chest pain and appears extremely anxious. She is diaphoretic and tachypneic with clear lung sounds. Assessment of the lower extremities shows right calf swelling. Oxygen saturation is 86% on room air.

h1.whyCorrect: Pleuritic (stabbing) pain is a hallmark of PE-induced lung infarction.

h5.whyCorrect: Unilateral swelling is the primary indicator of the source-clot (DVT).

h6.whyCorrect: Refractory hypoxemia is the primary physiological threat.

h2.whyIncorrect: Anxiety is a non-specific 'impending doom' feeling common to many emergencies.

h3.whyIncorrect: Diaphoresis is a general sympathetic response.

h4.whyIncorrect: Tachypnea is a compensatory sign rather than a diagnostic one for emboli.

rationale.answerAnalysis: The combination of pleuritic pain, calf swelling (source), and severe hypoxia defines the embolic picture.

screens.prompt: For each finding, indicate whether it is consistent with Pulmonary Embolism or Acute MI.

rows.text: Sharp, pleuritic pain worsened by breathing.
rows.rationale: PE pain is pleuritic (distal infarction); MI pain is usually pressure-like.
Clear lungs + hypoxia = V/Q mismatch (PE); MI often leads to crackles (HF).
Hyperventilation in early PE blows off CO2, causing alkalosis.
While PE causes minor elevation, significant rise is diagnostic for MI.

rationale.answerAnalysis: Differentiating between pulmonary and cardiac chest pain is a critical Level 5 skill.

screens.prompt: Complete the statement regarding priority nursing actions.

sentences.text: The nurse should initially place the patient on %{d1} and then prepare for %{d2} once the diagnosis is confirmed.

d1.whyCorrect: Hypoxemia is the immediate threat; NRB is required for 86% saturation.

distractorRationales.Mechanical ventilation: Premature; non-invasive support should be tried first.

d2.whyCorrect: Heparin stops the growth of the clot, allowing the body's natural fibrinolysis to work.

distractorRationales.Warfarin therapy: Too slow; takes days to reach therapeutic levels.
distractorRationales.Aspirin 325mg: Inadequate for a large arterial pulmonary clot.
